meta.title: Heatmap
meta.run_summary: No new cards; 4 cards updated. The most useful finding is DLR's measured printed gyroid radiator for fuel-cell aircraft: about 1.6 kW/kg against a 10 kW/kg target, and beaten overall by a louvered-fin core on pressure drop. Also added: Thales Alenia Space's modular printed gyroid exchanger for crewed space modules, printed heat pipes designed for powder removal, and the NATHENA project. Several publisher pages were blocked and Gateway to Research returned nothing. The website got today's report, but votes and comments left there were not read back this run (that step was blocked by a permission check).

coverage.datacentre: Good coverage of cold plates, jet impingement and heat reuse. One UK chip-level start-up found so far (Infiniflux).
coverage.aerospace: Strong on oil coolers and hydrogen. Cabin-air systems are now covered through Honeywell's STRATA project, and a measured printed pre-cooler core (Maryland) now gives one data point, but precooler-specific news is still rare. Defence aircraft electronics cooling now appears through BAE Systems' work with Leeds.
coverage.motorsport: Teams publish little, so most evidence comes from suppliers (Conflux, PWR) and student teams. Henry's steer here will help most.
coverage.other: Found by searching from the technology first: heat pipes, laser texturing, modelling, TPMS tests, fusion and transpiration cooling, and now laser-textured surfaces for radiating heat in space. Links to the three areas are mostly inferred.

cards.headline: Light air radiators for megawatt fuel-cell aircraft, which FlyZero calls a UK opportunity
cards.problem: Fuel-cell aircraft must reject megawatts of low-grade heat (stacks at about 80 C), and radiators can dominate weight and drag.
cards.technology: Compact air radiators: microtube, TPMS lattice and printed cores, targeting 5 to over 20 kW/kg.
cards.why: FlyZero names fuel-cell air radiators as the biggest thermal challenge for hydrogen aircraft, and its UK capability report calls 'novel air radiator heat exchangers with a commercially attractive manufacturing method' a high-opportunity area for the UK. Several designs compete: Reaction Engines' microtube radiator on Project FRESSON (claimed over 300 kW), DLR's printed TPMS exchangers (TRL 4) and Conflux's printed exchanger for Airbus ZEROe, now under technology readiness assessment (though ZEROe has slipped well into the 2030s). Where the radiator sits matters as much as the core: a Buffalo, Georgia Tech and Florida State model found a ducted radiator copes in most flight phases but not at takeoff, TU Wien is designing exchangers into a fan nacelle to win back some drag as thrust, and FEV with RWTH Aachen warns that bigger radiators add both mass and drag for eVTOL fuel cells. That FlyZero phrase, a compact core plus a way to make it, reads almost like an MTC mission statement. DLR's first measured printed core shows how far there is to go: its gyroid-pipe radiator moved up to 6.2 kW but managed about 1.6 kW/kg against a 10 kW/kg target, and a conventional louvered-fin core beat it overall because the gyroid lost more pressure (April 2026). Stretching the gyroid along the airflow helped, so the gap is a design and manufacturing problem rather than a dead end.

applicability.reason: All sources target fuel-cell aircraft thermal management.

trl.reason: DLR at TRL 4; FlyZero puts the global best at TRL 5 on a rig.

cards.barriers: Target kW/kg is far above today's radiators, takeoff on a hot day sets the size, and hydrogen aircraft timelines keep slipping.
cards.next_step: Talk to Cranfield Aerospace Solutions about what FRESSON's radiator relies on now that Reaction Engines is in administration.

cards.headline: Printed compact air-oil coolers for geared ultra-high-bypass engines
cards.problem: Geared and UHBR turbofans reject more oil heat, with less space for coolers and a fuel-burn penalty for every bit of drag.
cards.technology: Additively manufactured compact air-oil heat exchangers, including curved coolers that conform to the engine.
cards.why: This is the oil-cooler brief exactly, and the UK is strong in it. Meggitt (now Parker Meggitt) and TWI ran C-ALM AOHE to build an 80 kW, under-10 kg printed air-oil cooler for geared UHBR engines, aiming at TRL 6 and MRL 6, and published a review of L-PBF aluminium heat exchangers with Birmingham. Safran's HIPEX shows the payoff: a printed curved cooler, claimed to halve drag and save up to 1% fuel, already ground-tested on an engine. The one published like-for-like test is a caution: Penn State's printed AlSi10Mg copy of an aircraft oil cooler moved about 10-14% more heat but doubled the air-side pressure drop, and showed rough surfaces and edge cracks at fin joints. A 2026 Shenyang Aerospace University simulation extends the idea to cooled cooling air, where airfoil-shaped pin fins in a microchannel air-oil exchanger gave the best heat transfer for the least pressure loss.

applicability.reason: Both projects target turbofan oil cooling.

trl.reason: C-ALM targeted TRL 6; HIPEX has completed engine ground tests.

cards.barriers: Flight certification of printed aluminium heat exchangers; fatigue and fouling data; powder removal from fine fins.
cards.next_step: Ask TWI and Parker Meggitt what limited C-ALM's final TRL and MRL, and whether inspecting internal passages was the blocker. MTC metrology could fill that gap.

cards.headline: 3D-printed passive two-phase evaporators that cool chips with no pumps or fans
cards.problem: Cooling energy in data centres and HPC (pumps, fans, chillers), and low-grade waste heat that is hard to reuse.
cards.technology: Passive two-phase thermosiphon evaporator (vapour chamber) printed as one aluminium part.
cards.why: DTI and Heatflow printed the evaporator in one piece by laser powder bed fusion, which removes joints and leak paths, and tested it at 600 W, 50% above target, with no pumps or fans. Heat leaves at 60-80 C, warm enough for district heating, which ties it to the UK heat-network push. A Villanova University rack-scale thermosyphon gives a measured benchmark for the passive approach: stable from 2 to 7.5 kW per rack with no pump. It is still the clearest Venn centre found: the advance exists because of how the part is made. At server scale, EPFL and Nokia Bell Labs ran a 7 cm thermosyphon inside a 2U server at up to 240 W, so the pump-free route fits standard hardware. The machine maker Nikon SLM Solutions is now using this part (printed on its SLM280) to sell metal printing to data centres, a sign suppliers see a market.

applicability.reason: The project itself targets data-centre and HPC cooling.

trl.reason: Tested demonstrator at component level; no deployment yet.

cards.barriers: 600 W per device is below today's 1 kW+ GPUs; scale-up and long-term fluid compatibility of printed aluminium are unproven.
cards.next_step: Ask DTI about their PBF-LB parameters and leak testing for thin-wall two-phase parts. An RTO-to-RTO comparison of printed evaporator quality would be a natural first conversation.

cards.headline: Configurable printed oil coolers, race-proven and now in a production hypercar
cards.problem: Teams need custom heat exchangers quickly, inside a fixed envelope.
cards.technology: Parametric (configurable) printed heat-exchanger cores.
cards.why: A Conflux transmission oil cooler, built in two weeks on its configurable core platform, finished a full endurance race on a Multimatic car with about 20% more heat rejection than the incumbent in the same space. Pagani has since signed a six-year production contract for Conflux heat exchangers in the Utopia's Xtrac seven-speed gearbox, after track, road and thermal-shock trials; Conflux claims 30% more heat rejection, with no data published. Configurable cores turn heat-exchanger design into choosing parameters, which suits low-volume work in motorsport and aerospace, and Conflux and Xtrac both have UK operations.

applicability.reason: Race-proven in motorsport.

trl.reason: Completed an endurance race and contracted for a production hypercar.

cards.barriers: Cost per part; performance figures are company claims.
cards.next_step: Ask Xtrac (UK) how the Utopia gearbox cooler was tested, and Conflux's UK hub whether the platform has been tried for aerospace oil coolers.

cards.headline: Inspecting and qualifying printed heat exchangers: the gap FlyZero names
cards.problem: Printed heat exchangers cannot fly until internal passages, thin walls and joints can be inspected and lifed.
cards.technology: NDT and qualification of AM heat-exchanger cores: CT, leak testing, thin-wall property data, repeatable joints.
cards.why: FlyZero's roadmap lists the enablers for hydrogen heat exchangers and most are manufacturing problems: no thin-wall property data, bespoke assembly tooling, a need for automated NDT and repeatable joints, and qualification of AM materials from -253 C to 500 C. Its capability report says lifing printed heat exchangers is still a challenge, with HVM Catapult (MTC) and TWI studying AM and automated laser welding. The same gaps hold back printed oil coolers for today's engines, so the work pays off before hydrogen arrives. Clean internal passages are part of the same gap: MTC and Meggitt showed up to 99% of powder could be drained from sub-millimetre AlSi10Mg channels, with the last 1% still unsolved, and Birmingham found ultrasonic and vacuum-boiling methods clear deep L-PBF channels that grit-blasting can't. Birmingham's 2023 review adds that today's L-PBF systems aren't yet ready for the thin, leak-proof walls these parts need.

applicability.reason: FlyZero states these gaps for hydrogen aircraft; that they also apply to today's oil coolers is our inference.

trl.reason: Gaps identified; no qualification route yet.

cards.barriers: Needs a programme sponsor; qualification data is slow and costly to generate.
cards.next_step: A strong candidate for MTC's own roadmap. Check whether the ATI has funded follow-up to these FlyZero gaps since 2022.

cards.headline: AI-designed, printed cabin-air system parts, led from Honeywell's Yeovil site
cards.problem: Aircraft environmental control and cabin pressure systems rely on brazed heat exchangers and valves, and the UK wants to make the next generation here.
cards.technology: AM compact heat exchangers with heat-transfer surface features designed in, plus AI-driven physics simulation and a factory digital twin for series metal AM.
cards.why: Honeywell leads STRATA, a £14.1M ATI Programme project run from its Yeovil site, to develop five environmental control and cabin pressure control components with AM and AI simulation. The partners are all UK and mostly small: 3T Additive Manufacturing (series metal AM and a factory digital twin), BeyondMath (physics simulation), Qdot Technology (an Oxford spin-out making AM heat exchangers) and the Oxford Thermofluids Institute, which will work on surface features that raise heat transfer. No performance data is out yet. This is the closest match so far to the cabin-air brief, and it sits squarely on MTC's AM, inspection and design-for-manufacture work.

applicability.reason: The project targets aircraft environmental control and cabin pressure systems.

trl.reason: Announced August 2025; components in development, no test results yet.

cards.barriers: Flight certification of printed air-system parts; no results public yet.
cards.next_step: Ask the ATI or Honeywell Yeovil whether STRATA needs inspection or qualification support, and meet Qdot.

cards.headline: Fine-feature copper cold plates matched to each chip's heat map
cards.problem: AI chips above 1 kW, in racks heading for 600 kW, outgrow machined microchannel cold plates.
cards.technology: Copper cold plates with 30-70 micron features concentrated where the chip runs hottest.
cards.why: Three start-ups reach the same goal by different routes. Fabric8Labs prints copper electrochemically at 33 microns, Corintis designs microchannels about 70 µm wide in software and has made over 10,000 copper cold plates, aiming for a million by the end of 2026 (in a Microsoft test, three times better heat removal), and Alloy Enterprises laser-cuts copper sheets and diffusion bonds them. MTC covers both the additive and the laser routes, so it could benchmark them fairly. Green-laser printers for pure copper are also scaling: China's Addireen says it can now build 50 machines a month, aimed at cold plates (its figures). Independent numbers are starting to appear: Microsoft's test of Corintis plates, and a University of Illinois study in which a topology-optimised plate printed by Fabric8Labs gave up to 32% better cooling, or 68% lower pressure drop, than rectangular fins.

applicability.reason: All three companies sell into AI data-centre cooling.

trl.reason: Corintis has shipped over 10,000 plates and Fabric8Labs is in Wiwynn products; Alloy is earlier.

cards.barriers: Cost per plate against skived and machined copper, and proving no fouling or leaks over years of service.
cards.next_step: Corintis is the most mature and is in Switzerland. Ask what limits their volume route, and whether they want an independent test partner in Europe.

cards.headline: Printed loop and pulsating heat pipes with the wick built in
cards.problem: Spacecraft and dense electronics need passive cooling that moves heat with no pump, and wicks and fine channels are hard to make.
cards.technology: Loop heat pipes whose evaporator and wick are printed as one part, and pulsating heat pipes printed in pure copper.
cards.why: Advanced Cooling Technologies prints the stainless-steel evaporator and primary wick of its loop heat pipes as one LPBF part. A test unit on ammonia reached 5.1 W/K and ran stable at 125 W before drying out at 130-140 W, and a 15 W unit for a NASA CubeSat is built and awaiting thermal-vacuum tests, with 50 W to 1 kW designs to follow. Calyos and Beamler have printed a pure-copper pulsating heat pipe, so far without published data. Printed wicks depend on porosity control, which is MTC process and inspection work, and the same parts could serve data-centre and aircraft electronics. The University of Brighton has shown even resin-printed pulsating heat pipes work (1.7 °C/W at 30 W), and the von Karman Institute is testing printed-wick loop heat pipes under 2g for avionics boxes. Two 2025-26 papers show how such parts get tested for aircraft and space: Beihang and the University of Hertfordshire ran a see-through loop heat pipe at 30-150 W and 1-15 g and found start-up depends on the direction of the load, and an ESA-funded team including Brighton and Liverpool used infrared thermography with automatic tracking to follow flow inside pulsating heat pipes as gravity changes. An older ORNL-linked result shows printing can help the wick as well as the shape: a four-layer Ti-6Al-4V oscillating heat pipe printed in one piece worked up to 50 W in every orientation, with sintered powder on the channel walls acting as a second wick. Getting powder out is part of the design: the University of Missouri printed a looped oscillating heat pipe with a water-block heat sink on top and built de-powdering routes into the channels (prototype, no performance data yet). In Italy, Argotec and Prima Industrie plan printed pulsating heat pipes that double as a CubeSat's structure.

applicability.reason: The sources target spacecraft; use in data centres and aircraft electronics is our inference.

trl.reason: Test unit measured; flight unit built but not yet tested.

cards.barriers: Space qualification, and porosity control in printed wicks.
cards.next_step: Ask Brunel's Heat Pipe and Thermal Management group, the main UK academic heat-pipe team found so far, whether it has tried printed wicks.

cards.headline: Software that grows cold-plate channels for one specific chip
cards.problem: Hot spots on large AI packages such as the Nvidia GB200 set the peak temperature and limit performance.
cards.technology: Generative (reaction-diffusion) channel design coupled to a thermal model.
cards.why: University of Michigan-Dearborn's simulation cut peak temperature by over 35 C against a parallel-channel plate, and design software is already sold (Diabatix ColdStream; Ansys now shows AI geometry search for a 650 W GPU plate, simulation only). MTC has already done this end to end: with ToffeeX it generated, printed in CP1 aluminium and rig-tested an electronics cold plate stated to be 48% lighter with half the pressure drop and a 12% lower peak junction temperature than a serpentine design, though the case study doesn't say which figures were measured. Measured results are now appearing elsewhere too: Beihang printed a topology-optimised heat sink by laser melting and, in tests against copper foam, honeycomb and lattice sinks, it held temperature 15-155% longer and cut chip-to-chip temperature spread by over 11%. That makes this a capability MTC can point to, not just a gap: the next step is applying it to AI-chip cold plates and publishing measured results against tolerances and surface finish. The method is spreading fast in simulation: a 2026 preprint grows channel layouts for NVIDIA's GB200 superchip from its heat map, and Huazhong University with server maker Inspur blends topology-optimised regions with straight microchannels; neither has built a part.

applicability.reason: The paper targets the GB200 directly; the manufacturing route is our inference.

trl.reason: Measured prototypes at Beihang and MTC; AI-chip cold plates still mostly simulated.

cards.barriers: Simulated gains often shrink once minimum wall thickness, powder removal and roughness are applied.
cards.next_step: Ask MTC's own team for the measured rig data from the ToffeeX cold plate, and whether it has been tried on a GPU-class heat load.

cards.headline: The UK's compact aero-engine heat exchanger programme, with MTC already a partner
cards.problem: Next-generation passenger engines need lighter, more compact heat exchangers.
cards.technology: Compact heat-exchanger design and manufacturing development, plus ducted installations validated in a full-scale wind tunnel.
cards.why: An ATI-funded £7.4m programme runs from Meggitt's Midlands Thermal Management Centre of Excellence with AMRC, AFRC, the MTC, S&C Thermal Fluids and Cranfield. A related ATI case study (DBAHX, £0.87m) shows Parker Meggitt validating a ducted heat exchanger in a full-scale wind tunnel with a printed ejector. MTC is already inside this, so the roadmap value is knowing what was learnt and who at MTC holds it. S&C Thermal Fluids is a small UK firm worth knowing.

applicability.reason: The programme targets aero-engine heat exchangers.

trl.reason: Wind-tunnel validation for DBAHX; programme results not public.

cards.barriers: Results are not public and the IP sits with Parker Meggitt.
cards.next_step: Start inside MTC: find who worked on this programme, then ask Parker Meggitt about the next phase.

cards.headline: A fast model that corrects for the rough channels in printed heat exchangers
cards.problem: Standard design models underestimate pressure drop in printed heat exchangers by up to 26%, so parts miss their targets.
cards.technology: A reduced-order thermo-hydraulic model with a correction for melt dross in printed channels, fast enough for multi-objective optimisation.
cards.why: The University of Bath and Politecnico di Torino built a cheap thermo-hydraulic model of printed compact heat exchangers and checked it against published experiments. Temperature change was within 3.7%, but standard models underestimated pressure drop by up to 26.4%; correcting channel diameter for melt dross cut that to 11.4%, and a calibrated penalty factor to 4.3%. It applies to every printed heat exchanger on this page, and MTC could supply what the model needs most: measured channel geometry and roughness from CT. Related work on design rules is growing: an August 2026 Applied Thermal Engineering paper proposes quasi-fractal headers to share flow evenly in parameterised printed heat exchangers. Roughness is now being studied for lattice cores too: Dalian University of Technology and the Beijing Institute of Power Machinery published in 2026 on how surface roughness changes IWP-type TPMS heat exchangers.

applicability.reason: The paper names fuel-cell and battery cooling in transport; its use for aero and data-centre parts is ours.

trl.reason: Model validated against literature data, not new tests.

cards.barriers: The penalty factor is calibrated on a few datasets and may not carry across machines and alloys.
cards.next_step: Contact the Bath authors about validating the dross correction with CT data from MTC builds.

cards.headline: Designing liquid cooling for total energy, pump work included: an F1 lesson
cards.problem: Liquid-cooling energy is dominated by pumping across thousands of cold plates, not by the cold plates' heat transfer.
cards.technology: Low-pressure-drop printed cold plates designed with CFD and system-level models.
cards.why: Conflux, led by a former F1 engineer, argues the right measure is thermal resistance per unit of pump power, and quotes 0.0076 C/W at 6 L/min for its printed plates. Henry rated this the best example in the calibration set. It is an opinion piece with one vendor number, which holds the evidence score back, but the motorsport-to-data-centre transfer is exactly the cross-area link the tool should surface. Conflux is opening a UK hub, and its chairman Michael Fuller is still making the F1-to-data-centre case in the trade press (July 2026, no new figures).

applicability.reason: The article is written for data-centre cooling buyers.

trl.reason: Conflux sells cold plates; the system-level claim is not independently tested.

cards.barriers: No independent comparison; buyers rarely specify pump energy at component level.
cards.next_step: Conflux's new UK hub is the easy route in. Ask whether they would share test data comparing pump power against a conventional plate.

cards.headline: Using cryogenic hydrogen fuel as the heat sink in a turbofan
cards.problem: Hydrogen gas turbines must heat fuel from -253 C to injection temperature, and can use that cold to cool the engine.
cards.technology: Fuel-to-oil, intercooler and recuperator heat exchangers with cryogenic hydrogen as the coolant.
cards.why: Chalmers and GKN reported almost 8% lower take-off fuel burn and 37% lower NOx by cooling engine parts with hydrogen and preheating it with exhaust heat. Oxford's £9.5m EPSRC programme, with Imperial and Loughborough and backed by Rolls-Royce, Airbus and Parker, is building heat-transfer data for cryogenic fuel lines. FlyZero rates cryogenic heat exchangers at TRL 3 globally, held back by materials data, sealing and test facilities, and says UK firms go to the US to test. Europe does have one such rig: DLR's Future Propulsion Test Facility validates exhaust-heated hydrogen evaporators at TRL 3-6 (hydrogen gas to 250 bar, air to 700 °C), using liquid nitrogen in place of hydrogen for now.

applicability.reason: All sources target hydrogen aero engines.

trl.reason: Rig tests and modelling; FlyZero puts the global state at TRL 3.

cards.barriers: No large UK cryogenic hydrogen test facility; little hydrogen-embrittlement data for printed alloys.
cards.next_step: The Oxford programme has industry supporters and studentships; ask whether it needs manufacturing partners for test articles.

cards.headline: Printed heat exchangers for the hottest walls of UK fusion plants
cards.problem: Fusion plants such as UKAEA's STEP must remove extreme heat from divertor and chamber walls.
cards.technology: Metal-AM recuperative heat exchangers built into the wall, and printed copper and tungsten divertor parts tested under high heat flux.
cards.why: UKAEA funded four firms to design a heat exchanger for the hottest zone of STEP's chamber wall and judged the Element and HiETA design the most promising; HiETA printed a test piece within three months. Separately, UKAEA's HIVE rig at Culham (45 kW induction heating) has compared printed and machined copper and tungsten divertor prototypes. Neither source publishes figures. It is outside the three areas, but it is a UK programme using UK printed heat-exchanger makers, and fusion is on Henry's list of interesting heat-exchanger work.

applicability.reason: Both main sources are about fusion heat removal.

trl.reason: Test piece printed; prototypes tested in a small rig.

cards.barriers: Long timescales, and no published performance data yet.
cards.next_step: Ask UKAEA what followed the four design contracts, and whether HIVE could test MTC-printed parts.

cards.headline: Racing-approved alloys and print parameters for thin-wall heat exchangers
cards.problem: Printed heat exchangers need alloys that stay strong when hot and print leak-tight at fine fin thickness.
cards.technology: Aheadd CP1 (Al-Fe-Zr) heat-exchanger alloy with qualified L-PBF parameter sets.
cards.why: Constellium's Aheadd CP1 was approved for F1 in 2023, and PWR qualified it on Velo3D printers at 100-micron layers and has supplied printed heat exchangers in it since 2024. Eplus3D's parameters reach 99.93% density with leak-tight thin tube walls. This is the motorsport version of the aerospace qualification problem, already solved at racing scale, and PWR has a UK manufacturing site in Rugby. Parameter development and density and leak verification for heat-exchanger alloys is core MTC work, and the racing data could seed aerospace qualification.

applicability.reason: Approved and in use in F1.

trl.reason: In use in F1 since 2024.

cards.barriers: Aerospace material approval is a much higher bar; PWR and Constellium hold the know-how.
cards.next_step: Ask Constellium whether CP1 is being qualified for aerospace heat exchangers, and who is generating the data.

cards.headline: Printed liquid-nitrogen heat exchangers cool telescope instruments faster, a UK test of printed cryogenic parts
cards.problem: Cryogenic instruments and systems take a long time and a lot of liquid nitrogen to cool down, because conventional pre-cooling exchangers use only the boiling and waste the cold gas.
cards.technology: Additively manufactured liquid-nitrogen pre-cooling heat exchangers with extra evaporation area and internal structures that also take heat into the cold exhaust gas.
cards.why: The UK Astronomy Technology Centre and Royal Observatory Edinburgh built a small liquid-nitrogen pre-cooling rig for Extremely Large Telescope instruments and compared conventional and printed heat exchangers by how fast each cooled an instrumented mass. They report a clear cost and performance advantage for the printed units (UKRI-funded, July 2026, measured on a rig, figures in the paper). It is one of very few UK measured tests of printed cryogenic heat exchangers, and the same questions (thin walls at low temperature, using the cold gas as well as the boiling) come up in liquid-hydrogen fuel systems and airport liquefaction on the aerospace cards.

applicability.reason: The paper is about telescope instruments; the link to liquid-hydrogen aircraft and liquefaction is ours.

trl.reason: Measured on a lab-scale rig against conventional units.

cards.barriers: A niche first user, and nitrogen at 77 K is far milder than hydrogen at 20 K, so results won't carry over directly.
cards.next_step: Ask UK ATC which printing route and alloy they used and whether they would test parts at lower temperatures with MTC.

cards.headline: Binder-jetted lattice heat exchangers for making liquid hydrogen at airports
cards.problem: Hydrogen aircraft will need liquid hydrogen made at or near airports, and liquefaction heat exchangers are large and energy-hungry.
cards.technology: Cryogenic TPMS (gyroid-type) heat exchangers made by metal binder jetting.
cards.why: Qdot Technology, a UK SME, used a £45k Connected Places Catapult TRIG grant (2023) to design and make a TPMS cryogenic hydrogen heat exchanger by metal binder jetting. It sized the unit with end users, modelled TPMS unit cells and made test pieces, reaching TRL 2 to 3, and says early small-scale tests suggest 10-20% better performance, with no data published. Most printed heat exchangers use laser powder bed fusion, so a binder-jet route needs its own work on sintering shrinkage and porosity, which is MTC territory. Qdot is also a STRATA partner, which makes it a UK company to know. A Washington State printed liquefier heat exchanger is a warning: it delivered less than modelled because of the printed alloy's thermal properties and poor contact, which is exactly the data and joining work MTC could do.

applicability.reason: The project targets liquid-hydrogen production at airports.

trl.reason: As stated by the project; test pieces and a concept part made.

cards.barriers: A very small project so far; cryogenic testing at scale is still to come.
cards.next_step: Ask Qdot what happened after TRIG and whether binder-jet parts have been tested cold.

cards.headline: Laser-textured copper that boils far better, for two-phase cooling
cards.problem: Two-phase coolers (immersion tanks, evaporators, cold plates) are limited by how much heat a surface can boil off before it dries out.
cards.technology: Nanosecond laser texturing of copper in cross-hatch and checkerboard patterns.
cards.why: Researchers at Oak Ridge, Illinois and Kyushu laser-textured pure copper and measured pool boiling of water: critical heat flux rose about 56% and the boiling heat transfer coefficient about 730% against smooth copper. A second group now reports the same kind of gain in a device: the University of Ljubljana's laser-engineered copper raised critical heat flux by up to 118% in confined boiling and ran a 1 mm wick-free vapour chamber at 1.18 K/W at 40 W (FFHMT 2026). The obvious use is the boiling surfaces inside two-phase data-centre cold plates, vapour chambers and printed evaporators, and laser texturing is one of MTC's named capabilities. IRT Jules Verne's 3DCALOR project is also looking at textured surfaces for printed heat exchangers. Ljubljana's earlier work on laser-textured zirconium foils raised critical heat flux by 19-217% and heat transfer coefficients by 30-113%, measured with high-speed infrared thermography.

applicability.reason: The paper is about two-phase cooling in general; the data-centre link is ours.

trl.reason: Lab coupons, plus a working thin vapour chamber in Ljubljana.

cards.barriers: Mostly tested with water, not the dielectric fluids data centres use; long-term durability of the texture not reported.
cards.next_step: A small MTC texturing trial could check whether the gain holds with a dielectric fluid.

cards.headline: BAE Systems and Leeds want printed two-phase heat exchangers, sized fast, for aircraft electronics heat
cards.problem: Military and future aircraft carry more mission electronics, whose waste heat must be removed in very little space.
cards.technology: Additively manufactured single- and two-phase heat exchangers (evaporators, condensers, phase-change material) with fast sizing models.
cards.why: Two linked University of Leeds PhD projects with BAE Systems Warton aim to model two-phase aircraft heat exchangers, demonstrate design gains from additive layer manufacturing, and build fast sizing tools that run on a laptop instead of an HPC cluster. BAE offers its own facilities to build and test proof-of-concept parts. These are project plans with no results yet, but the idea has been shown to work: NLR's Clean Sky 2 TOPMOST loop, mostly printed in aluminium, cooled 2,400 W at 2.5 kg and held hotspots within 2 °C after vibration and salt-spray tests. It is a UK prime asking for exactly MTC's mix of AM, modelling and design for manufacture, and a two-phase aircraft heat exchanger is a natural partner to the oil-cooler and precooler cards.

applicability.reason: The projects name aircraft thermal management heat exchangers and AM demonstrators.

trl.reason: Leeds and BAE are at plan stage; NLR's printed loop reached a tested demonstrator in 2019.

cards.barriers: Defence context may limit what is published; two-phase behaviour in printed channels is poorly characterised.
cards.next_step: Ask Leeds (Duncan Borman) and BAE Systems Warton whether the demonstrators are built and who prints them.

cards.headline: Bypass-duct oil coolers: fin shapes measured against the drag they add
cards.problem: Geared ultra-high-bypass engines put a very high thermal load on gearbox oil, and coolers on the bypass duct wall add drag.
cards.technology: Optimised fin shapes for surface air-cooled oil coolers (SACOCs), designed numerically and measured in a reduced-scale wind tunnel.
cards.why: The Clean Sky 2 SACOC project (Universitat Politècnica de València with Safran Aircraft Engines, 2019 to 2021) built a numerical method and a reduced-scale wind tunnel for surface oil coolers. The measurements show the trade-off plainly: a finned cooler gave 171% more heat transfer than a flat plate but 192% more friction, and the project says its optimised fins add almost 20% heat exchange and 13% better airflow permeability. A 2025 review names AM fins as the next step, and fin shapes that trade heat against drag are what printing and laser processing can make. The UK now has its own handle on the installed problem: Cranfield University and Rolls-Royce (EPSRC-funded, May 2026) modelled a naturally ventilated air-oil cooler in a geared-fan bypass duct together with the exhaust, and found it could meet the take-off heat load for a 0.7% cruise-thrust penalty in their example. That gives a UK route to test whether printed or laser-made fins shift that trade-off. Rolls-Royce has already run an EU project on exactly this: SHEFAE 2 (2016-2021, €1.34m, with BTU Cottbus-Senftenberg) set out to make long, shallow surface coolers and their mountings and test them on Rolls-Royce demonstrator engines, though CORDIS publishes no results. The team's journal paper (2022, with Universidad Politécnica de Madrid and Safran) adds two useful results: fins shaped to cut pressure drop gave a 10% lower friction factor and a 5.2% higher overall heat transfer coefficient than standard trapezoidal fins, and the cooler only disturbs the bypass flow over about its own height and width, so a small rig with the right velocity profile is enough to test new fin designs.

applicability.reason: All sources are about turbofan oil cooling.

trl.reason: Validated in a reduced-scale wind tunnel, not on an engine.

cards.barriers: Every gain in heat transfer costs drag, and engine makers hold the installation data.
cards.next_step: Ask Cranfield's propulsion group (with Rolls-Royce) whether their bypass-duct model could score printed fin shapes, and read UPV's two 2022 IJHMT papers for the baseline fins.

cards.headline: Compact supercritical-CO2 heat exchangers for the UK's STEP fusion power plant
cards.problem: STEP has to move fusion heat into a supercritical CO2 power cycle, and later change load quickly, through very large, very compact heat exchangers.
cards.technology: Compact sCO2 heat exchangers: today's diffusion-bonded printed circuit heat exchangers (PCHEs), and laser-melted microchannel cores as a possible challenger.
cards.why: UK Industrial Fusion Solutions has chosen a transcritical CO2 cycle for STEP (100 MWe net, 2040s) and plans sCO2 cooling for some in-vessel parts, and its team has published a cost-and-performance optimisation of the cycle; its 2026 roadmap prefers PCHEs for their maturity and plans no big scale-up, but says exchangers still need testing under rapid load changes. Printing is starting to compete: a University of Maryland team laser-melted an sCO2 microchannel exchanger rated above 800 °C and 80 bar and measured 45.4 MW/m³, which it says is the most compact reported. Wisconsin's test of a PCHE for a 5 MWth microreactor shows what benchmark data looks like (325 °C, 10 MPa, fibre-optic temperature maps). For MTC the openings are dynamic testing and modelling, and making the case for printed cores against PCHEs. The incumbent is strong: Kelvion, for one, sells diffusion-bonded units it rates to 1,000 bar and 600 °C for hydrogen and sCO2 duty (company figures).

applicability.reason: STEP's paper names compact sCO2 heat exchangers and their dynamic testing as needs; the link to printed cores is ours, from the Maryland result.

trl.reason: PCHEs are mature at up to 50 MWth; printed sCO2 cores are lab-tested prototypes.

cards.barriers: PCHEs are the incumbent and STEP prefers them for maturity; printed cores have no high-pressure qualification record.
cards.next_step: Ask UKIFS what its proof-of-concept sCO2 rig will test and whether printed exchanger modules are in scope.

cards.headline: Megawatt-class thermal management for hybrid-electric regional aircraft
cards.problem: Hybrid-electric aircraft generate 300-1000 kW of waste heat, against 35-50 kW in similar aircraft today.
cards.technology: Air-cycle and vapour-cycle systems with printed air-to-air and air-to-liquid exchangers, developed with a digital twin.
cards.why: TheMa4HERA is a €33.5m Clean Aviation project led by Honeywell, aiming for TRL 5 in 2026 with a full-scale ground demonstrator at Fraunhofer. Conflux joined in 2025 to make printed exchangers, evaporators and condensers, and presented the printed air-cycle heat exchangers with Honeywell UK at Formnext 2025. The partner list (Liebherr, Collins, Calyos, DLR, NLR, plus UK partners Conflux UK, Honeywell UK and Element Digital Engineering) is a map of who matters in aircraft environmental control heat exchangers. NLR's earlier Clean Sky 2 project TOPMOST (2017-19) built pumped two-phase cooling loops with mostly printed aluminium parts for Thales power electronics: 2.5 kg, 2,400 W removed (twice the requirement) with hot spots within 2 °C, and vibration and salt-spray tests passed. Testing at this scale is scarce: SwRI in the US now markets heat exchanger tests up to several megawatts. TheMa4HERA now has a successor: OSYRYS, a €40m Clean Aviation project (2026-2030) led by Safran Electrical & Power, aims for a TRL 6 integrated demonstration of megawatt-level power, thermal and energy management for hybrid-electric regional aircraft, with Airbus, Liebherr, Thales, Collins, ATR and the UK's Goodrich Controls among 24 partners. An earlier Clean Sky 2 project, NATHENA (2018-2022, €1.5m), set out to print aluminium and Inconel air-air exchangers of up to 500 kW for hybrid propulsion, but no results are published on TRIMIS.

applicability.reason: The project targets aircraft thermal management.

trl.reason: TheMa4HERA aims at TRL 5 in 2026; its successor OSYRYS targets TRL 6 by 2030.

cards.barriers: Hybrid-electric regional aircraft entry into service is uncertain.
cards.next_step: Watch for TheMa4HERA results at the end of 2026. Calyos, a small Belgian two-phase company in the consortium, may be worth a call. Goodrich Controls (Collins, UK) is a partner in five EU hybrid-electric regional aircraft projects since 2023 (HECATE, OSYRYS, PHARES, HERACLES, LEIA), so it is the UK door into this work.

cards.headline: Liquid-hydrogen evaporators for hydrogen Le Mans cars
cards.problem: Hydrogen-engined endurance cars must boil off liquid hydrogen using engine coolant, without freezing the coolant, in a tight package.
cards.technology: A printed liquid-hydrogen-to-coolant heat exchanger (evaporator), developed against a digital twin of the fuel system.
cards.why: Dallara and Conflux have started a pre-study to co-develop a printed evaporator that warms liquid hydrogen with engine coolant, in line with the ACO's plan for hydrogen cars at Le Mans by 2030. Dallara is building a digital twin of the storage and delivery system, and the named problems are coolant freezing, hydrogen embrittlement and packaging. There are no results yet. It is the same cryogenic heat-exchanger problem as hydrogen aircraft, at racing pace, so work here could transfer both ways.

applicability.reason: The study targets hydrogen endurance racing.

trl.reason: Pre-study launched July 2026; simulation and hardware tests planned.

cards.barriers: Hydrogen racing dates keep moving, and printed alloys need cryogenic and embrittlement data.
cards.next_step: Ask Conflux's UK hub whether the evaporator shares know-how with its aerospace hydrogen work.

cards.headline: Printed heat exchangers for aircraft air systems and precoolers
cards.problem: Bleed-air precoolers and environmental control heat exchangers are brazed plate-fin assemblies with many joints, shaped by the space they must fit.
cards.technology: AM heat-exchanger cores with fewer joints and shapes fitted to the installation; software-generated precooler surfaces.
cards.why: Liebherr Aerospace, Europe's leading air-systems supplier, set the topic for NATHENA, a Clean Sky 2 project that built a scale-one printed aircraft heat exchanger with fewer welded and brazed parts and a shape fitted to the aircraft. LEAP 71 and Farsoon have since printed a 1.5 m precooler in one piece with software-generated surfaces, though it is a hypersonic concept with no data. Measured data exist too: a University of Maryland printed manifold-microchannel pre-cooler core with 165 µm fins handled 2.78 kW at 600 C, close to 10 kW/kg and up to 25% denser than plate-fin units (2018, small scale). This is the closest match yet to the precooler brief, and also the main coverage gap. The prize is volume: Liebherr alone makes nearly 12,000 air-conditioning heat exchangers a year and passed 100,000 in 2023, so a printed design that wins here needs a production route, not just a prototype.

applicability.reason: NATHENA targets civil aircraft heat exchangers; LEAP 71's precooler is for hypersonic, not turbofan, use.

trl.reason: Lab-tested proof of concept (NATHENA) and a concept print (LEAP 71).

cards.barriers: Brazed plate-fin precoolers are mature and cheap, so printed ones must win on weight or installation to justify qualification.
cards.next_step: Ask Liebherr Toulouse what happened after NATHENA and whether printed precoolers are on its roadmap.

cards.headline: F1's 2026 rules: more electric heat to reject, less air to do it
cards.problem: 2026 cars nearly triple MGU-K power to 350 kW while losing downforce and cooling airflow; active aero makes duct flow transient.
cards.technology: Low-temperature circuits for battery, MGU-K and electronics; non-rectangular heat exchangers; transient system models.
cards.why: Mercedes HPP says cooling must be designed into the aero concept from the start, and Modelon describes the shift from steady to transient thermal design as active aero changes duct flow. Oxford Brookes is modelling MGU-K heat losses under the new rules, and team sidepods show the result: tight wraps around heat exchangers and swappable cooling panels. The problem is clear; non-rectangular printed cores and transient models are where MTC fits. A rough sum shows the scale: a 350 kW MGU-K at 95% efficiency sheds about 17 kW, and the battery and inverters run on separate dielectric loops at about 50 °C, close enough to ambient that the radiators must grow (an F1 Chronicle estimate, not team data).

applicability.reason: All sources are about F1's 2026 cooling.

trl.reason: The cars race; the new design methods are less mature.

cards.barriers: Teams keep their solutions secret, and the market is small though influential.
cards.next_step: Oxford Brookes' motorsport group is the most open route into this problem.

cards.headline: Measured cryogenic properties of printed alloys, the missing data for liquid-hydrogen heat exchangers
cards.problem: Designers of liquid-hydrogen heat exchangers for aircraft have little data on how printed metals conduct and expand at -253 C, so designs underperform or are over-margined.
cards.technology: Cryogenic thermal conductivity, expansion and heat-capacity data for additively manufactured copper, Scalmalloy, Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718.
cards.why: KIT measured printed copper, Scalmalloy, Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718 from about 4 K to 300 K for AdHyBau, a German project on liquid-hydrogen-cooled electric aircraft drives with MT Aerospace and Siemens. Optimised laser-melted copper reached a residual resistance ratio of about 170, double the as-received powder's, and Scalmalloy conducts about ten times better than Inconel or titanium; the data feed a digital twin. FlyZero lists 'no thin-wall property data from -253 C' as a hydrogen enabler, and a US printed liquefier fell short partly for this reason. UK testing of the alloys MTC prints, in thin-wall form, would fill a named gap.

applicability.reason: The project targets LH2-cooled aircraft propulsion components.

trl.reason: Material data measured; no component yet.

cards.barriers: Cryogenic test capacity is scarce; properties depend on each machine's parameters and heat treatment.
cards.next_step: Check whether UK cryogenic test labs (for example at the STFC or university hydrogen centres) could measure MTC-printed thin-wall coupons.

cards.headline: Laser-melted gyroid micro heat exchangers with 100 µm features reach 12 kW/m²K
cards.problem: Chip and power-electronics cooling needs very high heat transfer in small volumes, beyond what conventional microchannels give.
cards.technology: Gyroid TPMS micro heat exchangers built by micro selective laser melting.
cards.why: Laserinstitut Hochschule Mittweida built three gyroid micro heat exchangers by micro selective laser melting, with features as small as 100 µm, and compared them with a microchannel unit. The abstract reports heat transfer coefficients up to 12 kW/(m²K), over 300% above conventional plate heat exchangers, and leak-free operation to 8 bar (abstract only; full paper not read). Feature sizes this small would suit printed cold plates for AI chips, though the paper does not say so. It puts laser process control, not just lattice design, at the centre.

applicability.reason: The paper is about micro heat exchangers generally; the link to chip cold plates is ours.

trl.reason: Lab prototypes measured.

cards.barriers: Micro-SLM build size and speed, powder removal from 100 µm channels, and fouling.
cards.next_step: Read the full Jena Laser Conference paper for test conditions and pressure drop.

cards.headline: Gyroid-core fuel-cooled oil coolers designed for printing
cards.problem: Fuel-cooled oil coolers must pass more heat in less volume while keeping fuel above icing temperature.
cards.technology: TPMS (gyroid) heat-exchanger cores designed with implicit modelling and CFD.
cards.why: nTop and Ansys show a full design workflow for a printed gyroid fuel-cooled oil cooler, based on an America Makes project, and Honeywell was testing printed fuel-oil exchangers as early as 2015. The design tools are now commodity. What is missing is test data showing gyroid cores beat plate-fin designs once pressure drop, fouling and inspection are counted, which is a build-and-test job. Printed fuel-oil exchangers are also edging towards production elsewhere: GA-ASI and Conflux signed an agreement in 2023 to take Conflux's flight-qualified printed fuel-oil heat exchangers into production on GA-ASI aircraft, though no performance figures were published. In the US, AFRL built a test rig for printed fuel-oil coolers in 2019 (UDRI with DRT Aerospace and GE, three coolers tested for pressure drop, temperatures and particulates) and said it would open it to industry; the UK has no equivalent public rig that this search found.

applicability.reason: The workflow targets aero-engine fuel-oil cooling.

trl.reason: Design and simulation for gyroid cores; Conflux's printed fuel-oil exchangers are stated to be flight-qualified.

cards.barriers: Fuel-side fouling and cleaning of TPMS passages.
cards.next_step: Conflux's UK hub is the nearest supplier with flight-qualified printed fuel-oil exchangers; ask what test evidence qualification needed.

cards.headline: Pumped two-phase direct-to-chip cooling for racks heading to 200 kW and beyond
cards.problem: Racks have gone from about 50 kW (2022) to 120-140 kW (2024), with 200-240 kW expected in 2026, and processors are passing 4 kW; single-phase water loops are running out of margin and water is scarce at many sites.
cards.technology: Two-phase evaporator cold plates on the chip, with a pumped dielectric refrigerant loop and enhanced boiling surfaces.
cards.why: ZutaCore raised $100m from Mitsubishi Electric, Carrier and Samsung and is in over 75 sites, so the market is real. The research has moved on this year: a Journal of Electronic Packaging paper sets out how to budget temperature across a pumped two-phase loop, St. Cloud State tested a refrigerant-to-liquid system for dense racks, Maryland (with Modelon) is building reduced-order design models for micropillar evaporators, and Michigan Tech with start-up Artmetics measured piezo micro-vibration pushing boiling on microstructured copper into a controlled flash-boiling regime. Advanced Cooling Technologies has shown what printing adds: a whole two-phase cold plate in one AlSi10Mg build, with a wick over each of seven hot spots and an internal phase separator, ran above 505 W/cm² at about 0.16 K·cm²/W on under 0.14 W of pumping. The evaporator is a fine-feature part whose boiling surface sets the limit, which is where MTC's printing, laser texturing and modelling all meet. A UK group is working on a related idea: the University of Warwick with ORE Catapult let water boil in microchannels under a power module only during short overloads, cutting thermal resistance when it matters most. Single-phase still leads for now: Motivair by Schneider Electric estimates single-phase cold plates hold about 55% of the 2026 liquid-cooling market, and the argument for two-phase in hot climates (condensing at desert ambient with no chillers) is so far a vendor view rather than a measured result.

applicability.reason: All sources target data-centre or AI chip cooling.

trl.reason: ZutaCore is deployed; the new evaporator and boiling-surface work is lab scale.

cards.barriers: Refrigerant choice under PFAS rules; servicing and leak detection; most of the new results are US preprints or abstracts so far.
cards.next_step: Check whether any UK group is working on two-phase evaporator surfaces; the Ljubljana and Oak Ridge laser-texturing results suggest a test MTC could run.

cards.headline: Printed battery cold plates, CT-checked, in a 2026 F1 power unit
cards.problem: 2026 power units carry much larger batteries and electronics; Honda says battery and motor thermal management will decide reliability.
cards.technology: AM battery cold plates and cooling plates with CT-based inspection.
cards.why: Ford has made around 1,000 printed parts for the 2026 Red Bull Ford power unit, including battery cold plates, and each one goes through strength tests, 3D scanning, X-ray and CT before metrology. Honda says battery and motor thermal management is where manufacturers will differ. Inspection at that rate is familiar MTC ground, and these cold plates are close cousins of data-centre ones. Formula E shows the trend: a Cranfield study finds each new car generation uses less energy but makes over 60% more battery heat, and above about 57 C the battery loses power fast.

applicability.reason: Both sources are about 2026 F1 power units.

trl.reason: Racing in 2026.

cards.barriers: Team-confidential; little public data.

cards.headline: Laser-textured graphite surfaces to radiate more heat from satellite electronics
cards.problem: Spacecraft can only shed heat by radiation, so processors are often run below their rating to stay cool.
cards.technology: Synthetic-graphite circuit boards that spread heat, plus ultrafast-laser surface textures that raise emissivity.
cards.why: Teledyne Labtech is leading the ATMS project with Bangor University, backed by Airbus Endeavr (Airbus and the Welsh Government), to make lightweight boards that spread heat through synthetic graphite and radiate it from laser-textured surfaces. Bangor uses ultrafast lasers to etch microscopic textures that should raise emissivity, but no measured values are published yet; prototypes are due by the end of 2026. It is a small UK team using laser texturing, one of MTC's named capabilities, on a different heat path from the boiling-surface card: radiation rather than boiling. Measuring emissivity and texture durability is the kind of metrology MTC could add.

applicability.reason: The project targets space electronics; use on terrestrial radiators would be our inference.

trl.reason: Project plan with prototype demonstrations due by end of 2026; no results yet.

cards.barriers: No emissivity data yet; textures must survive launch, thermal cycling and atomic oxygen, and space qualification is slow.
cards.next_step: Ask Bangor University which emissivity gains they have measured and whether texture durability testing is planned.

cards.headline: UK cooling money goes to facilities, not to chip-level cooling
cards.problem: UK cooling investment is concentrated in two firms, and chip-level cooling, where manufacturing matters most, has only one UK company named.
cards.technology: Chip-level cold plates and two-phase cooling.
cards.why: Tracxn counts $362m raised by UK cooling and heat-reuse firms, second only to the US, but almost all of it went to Deep Green and Iceotope, and it names one UK chip-level company, Infiniflux. Infiniflux turns out to be a London start-up founded in 2023 with two staff and $30,000 raised; it claims its package-integrated two-phase silicon cold plate cuts thermal resistance up to 4x, and it won a place in Taiwan's IC Taiwan Grand Challenge. UK demand is real (Imperial's first direct liquid-cooled cluster went live at Digital Realty's Woking site in 2025), so a thin UK supply base is a reason for an RTO to help.

applicability.reason: The report is about investment; the link to MTC manufacturing support is our inference.

trl.reason: Market signal, not a technology.

cards.barriers: The UK market for chip-level parts is small and US and Swiss start-ups are ahead.
cards.next_step: Call Infiniflux: it is tiny and claims a lot, so independent testing or prototype manufacture could be a fit.

cards.headline: GPU simulation cuts heat-exchanger design from months to two weeks
cards.problem: Heat-exchanger design and validation loops take months, which limits how many variants get tried.
cards.technology: GPU-accelerated conjugate heat-transfer CFD combined with implicit modelling.
cards.why: Sintavia ran a 30-million-cell conjugate heat-transfer model in seven minutes on Nvidia GPUs, 11 times faster than on CPUs, and designed a multi-circuit heat exchanger in two weeks. It claims 30% less weight and 20% better thermal efficiency, checked by CT scanning. Faster simulation means many variants a week instead of one a month, and MTC's modelling team could test whether the workflow holds for its own work. The gains are company claims. GKN Aerospace (its Swedish arm) and Chalmers have started BAIDHEX (SEK 6m, to 2028) to have machine learning generate bioinspired aero heat exchangers that already meet manufacturing rules.

applicability.reason: The heat exchanger is for aerospace.

trl.reason: Designed, printed and CT-checked; no published test data.

cards.barriers: Vendor claims; commercial CFD licensing on GPUs.

cards.headline: Jet-impingement cold plates aimed at chip hot spots
cards.problem: AI chips have hot spots of hundreds of W/cm², and conventional microchannel cold plates need high coolant flow to keep up.
cards.technology: Arrays of small coolant jets aimed at hot spots, in etched, machined or 3D-printed manifolds.
cards.why: Purdue and UCLA measured a heat transfer coefficient of 80 kW/m²K at 2.5 L/min with a 5 mm high jet manifold, and 3D printed a GPU-sized version in 316 stainless steel. Companies claim more: Frore says its LiquidJet plate runs Nvidia Rubin 6-12°C cooler on about a third less flow, JetCool (an MIT Lincoln Laboratory spin-out, $17m raised in 2023) claims 3-5x lower thermal resistance than microchannel plates, and Wiwynn reports 20-48% gains. Jet manifolds are full of small nozzles and internal plenums, which suits printing and needs careful inspection. Two more signs the manufacturing route is the point: the US DOE has extended Purdue's COOLERCHIPS project on two-phase jet impingement with printed, topology-optimised surfaces into durability testing, and Alloy Enterprises has filed a patent (May 2026) on jet manifolds made by stacking and bonding patterned metal sheets in one build.

applicability.reason: All sources target data-centre and AI chip cooling.

trl.reason: Lab-measured at Purdue; vendor products claimed but not independently tested.

cards.barriers: Most figures are vendor claims against unnamed baselines.
cards.next_step: Compare a printed jet manifold with a fine-feature copper plate on the same test chip.

cards.headline: Measured tests show gyroid heat exchangers mainly win on pressure drop
cards.problem: Printed TPMS (gyroid) heat exchangers are widely promoted, but like-for-like measured comparisons with conventional units are rare.
cards.technology: Gyroid TPMS cores made by metal AM, tested against a commercial brazed plate heat exchanger.
cards.why: Seoultech and the University of Akron tested a metal-printed gyroid heat exchanger against a commercial brazed plate unit: heat transfer at most 4.4% better, friction up to 30.5% lower, overall merit about 7% higher. Waseda University and AGC then showed that grading the lattice matters more than the lattice itself: varying wall position to balance hot and cold flow gave 28.7% more measured heat transfer than a uniform printed lattice. A US simulation study suggests other surface shapes can beat gyroids in turbulent air. Together they are a reality check on TPMS claims, and independent like-for-like testing of graded lattices is a service an RTO can offer. NYU Abu Dhabi and Toronto Metropolitan have since tested printed gyroid heat sinks at three porosities and split one gyroid into two separate fluid domains at different flow rates, matching COMSOL models. Boiling changes the picture: Seoul National University of Science and Technology measured printed aluminium gyroid and diamond channels with R-1234yf and found the gyroid gave up to 165% higher boiling heat transfer for up to 17.4% more pressure drop, while the diamond did better in single-phase flow. So the best lattice depends on whether the fluid boils, which matters for two-phase cold plates and evaporators. Beihang's simulations show the gyroid shape itself can be tuned, cutting pressure drop by 13% for slightly more heat transfer, but nothing was built. Xi'an Jiaotong University has also modelled and tested TPMS cold plates for electronics (Applied Energy, 2025). Two more measured cases point the same way. DLR's printed gyroid-pipe radiator for fuel-cell aircraft was smaller and lighter for its duty than a louvered-fin core but lost overall on pressure drop (2026). Politecnico di Torino, Thales Alenia Space and CIM4.0 printed a modular sheet-gyroid exchanger for crewed space modules, and its nine-module prototypes performed like an ideal counter-flow unit, so splitting a lattice core into printable modules does not cost performance.

applicability.reason: The tests are generic; their bearing on the aerospace and data-centre TPMS cards is ours.

trl.reason: Lab-tested against a commercial unit.

cards.barriers: One measured comparison; results depend on fluid, flow range and cell size.
cards.next_step: Use as a benchmark when judging TPMS performance claims.

orgs.name: Seoul National University of Science and Technology
University of the District of Columbia

cards.headline: Printed brake ducts for faster development under new FIA limits
cards.problem: Brake discs over 700 C must be cooled within FIA duct rules, now with devices that heat or cool wheels and brakes banned.
cards.technology: Simulation-led brake-duct design with printed prototypes and carbon-PEEK race parts.
cards.why: Cadillac F1 prints brake-duct prototypes to check its simulations, and Visa Cash App RB prints race ducts in carbon-fibre PEEK on Roboze machines, cutting lead time by 66%. The FIA ban moves the job back to duct geometry. Siemens has shown adjoint topology optimisation in Simcenter STAR-CCM+ that shapes a duct to maximise heat transfer to the rotor within volume and pressure-drop limits, with printing as the way to make it, though it published no gains. Polymer AM is mature here, so novelty is modest; the open question is whether optimised duct shapes are worth it under the new limits.

applicability.reason: All sources are about F1 brake cooling.

trl.reason: In use on race cars.

cards.barriers: Low novelty and well served by existing suppliers.

cards.headline: Sheffield's Iceotope scales sealed-chassis liquid cooling
cards.problem: Energy and water use of air-cooled data centres as AI racks densify.
cards.technology: Sealed-chassis precision immersion using a small volume of dielectric coolant.
cards.why: Iceotope holds over 200 patents, claims up to 40% lower energy and 96% lower water use, and raised a $26m Series B in May 2026 to scale its KUL AI racks.  It has had UK public backing before: British Patient Capital put £5m into its 2022 round. Its next challenge is making sealed chassis at volume, which is an assembly and manufacturing problem more than a physics one. It is a UK company close to MTC's patch, though the performance figures are its own. Castrol is another UK player: it planned immersion test facilities at Pangbourne with Submer tanks (2022), and a 2026 paper with UIUC and Imperial gives a property-based figure of merit for choosing single-phase immersion fluids, checked on a MOSFET test rig.

applicability.reason: Iceotope sells data-centre cooling.

trl.reason: Products on sale; performance claims not independently verified.

cards.barriers: Dielectric fluid supply and PFAS rules; chassis must suit many server designs.
cards.next_step: Ask Iceotope where its production bottleneck is as it scales after the Series B; it has led or partnered on three Innovate UK and ISCF projects since 2022, including the £2.5m Enhanced Liquid Immersion Power Systems project.

cards.headline: Where the UK's microtube heat-exchanger know-how went after Reaction Engines
cards.problem: The UK's leading microtube precooler developer went into administration in October 2024.
cards.technology: Microtube precoolers and radiators (SABRE precooler, FRESSON fuel-cell radiator).
cards.why: Reaction Engines made very fine-tube heat exchangers that cooled hypersonic intake air, were used in F1 cooling and were chosen for the FRESSON fuel-cell radiator. Administrators were selling the IP in 2025 with a preferred bidder in exclusivity. FlyZero listed Reaction Engines as a UK strength, so where the IP and people went matters for UK capability. Joining and assembling thousands of microtubes is a joining and automation problem MTC knows. Others are still working the problems the SABRE precooler faced: Beihang published in 2026 on how frost forms in microtube precoolers and an anti-frost injection method. The capability being sold was real: in 2019 the UK-built precooler quenched air above 1,000 °C in under 1/20th of a second at Mach 5 conditions in tests backed by DARPA, the UK Space Agency and ESA.

applicability.reason: The sources are business news; the link to MTC joining and automation is our inference.

trl.reason: Precooler tested in 2019; radiator claimed for FRESSON.

cards.barriers: Unclear who owns the IP now.
cards.next_step: Find out who bought the IP; a new owner may be looking for manufacturing partners.

cards.headline: Printed motor and inverter cooling in student electric race cars
cards.problem: Electric race powertrains overheat over an endurance run, and multi-part cooling jackets leak.
cards.technology: Single-piece printed aluminium motor jackets and cold plates with integrated mounts and internal flow guides.
cards.why: Esslingen's E-Stall Formula Student team replaced a leak-prone two-part polymer jacket with a printed aluminium motor jacket and inverter plate from Eplus3D, and says motors and inverters stayed below 65°C, against 120°C the season before (team account, method not given). Puntozero redesigned the power-electronics cold plate of the Dynamis PRC car for AM, claiming 25% less weight and 300% more heat-transfer area. Student teams are a cheap, fast way to get printed cooling parts onto a track, and Formula Student runs in the UK too.

applicability.reason: Both are race-car cooling parts.

trl.reason: Raced at student competitions.

cards.barriers: Student scale; results are team-reported.
cards.next_step: A UK Formula Student team could be a low-cost test bed for MTC-printed cooling parts.

cards.headline: Getting data-centre heat into UK heat networks
cards.problem: UK data-centre growth (NESO: 35 TWh a year by 2050, about 40% for cooling) and the need to decarbonise heat.
cards.technology: Heat recovery at 25-40 C, raised to 55-80 C by heat pumps or by liquid cooling that runs hotter.
cards.why: Policy and money are lining up. DESNZ put £90m into heat networks fed by data centres, Deep Green has approval for a 5.6 MW site in Bradford, EnergiRaven models enough heat for 3.5-6.3m homes by 2035, and a 2026 Scottish Enterprise review says one large site could yield hundreds of GWh of heat a year and should favour closed-loop cooling over evaporative. The DESNZ pipeline names actual schemes, such as Hemiko's Tyseley network in Birmingham taking heat from a 2.5 MW data centre for 21 buildings. MTC's angle is upstream, and a Rijeka simulation shows why: direct liquid cooling loops at 25-30 °C still need heat pumps for older networks, so the hotter the coolant leaves the chip, the less heat-pump work is needed, which favours two-phase and printed cold plates that run warm. Strong on UK relevance, weaker on a direct MTC role. In London, Old Oak & Park Royal Development Corporation chose Hemiko to build a network on heat from data centres including Vantage's two local campuses, which the partners say will supply up to 95 GWh a year to 9,000 new homes and businesses and Central Middlesex Hospital, with five expansions planned to 2040.

applicability.reason: None of these sources mention manufacturing; the link through hotter-running cold plates is ours.

trl.reason: Heat networks are mature; high-temperature chip cooling is not.

cards.barriers: Data centres are rarely near heat demand, and heat-supply contracts are slow.
cards.next_step: Watch the DESNZ-funded schemes for the coolant temperatures they specify.

cards.headline: Printed porous walls for transpiration cooling, where print defects decide performance
cards.problem: Gas-turbine hot parts need more cooling for less air than film cooling allows.
cards.technology: Transpiration (porous or effusion) cooling through printed perforated, TPMS and graded-porosity walls.
cards.why: A 2025 Shanghai Jiao Tong University review collects the evidence: well-designed transpiration cooling reaches up to five times the cooling effectiveness of film cooling. But printing changes the part: perforated designs with 0.5-0.06 mm holes lost 4-77% of their porosity, defects cut permeability by 15% and strength by 10%. Transpiration cooling is on Henry's keyword list, and the gap between the designed and printed part is a metrology and process-control problem MTC knows well. A 2026 University of Central Florida thesis adds a design rule worth testing: in its model, thermal-stress yielding in transpiration walls falls as porosity rises, while local deformation becomes the risk. DLR is doing the process side: it printed VDM780 superalloy porous walls, setting porosity through laser parameters, and measured pressure loss and how evenly coolant comes out (EUCASS 2025, no figures published).

applicability.reason: The review is about gas-turbine cooling.

trl.reason: Lab rigs in the cited studies.

cards.barriers: Second-hand review; porosity control in very fine printed holes.
cards.next_step: Look for UK groups working on printed effusion cooling, starting with the Oxford Thermofluids Institute.

cards.headline: Two-phase immersion cooling coupled straight into a heat pump
cards.problem: Reusing hyperscale (over 50 MW) data-centre heat at useful temperatures.
cards.technology: Two-phase immersion with the coolant condensing directly in a natural-refrigerant heat pump.
cards.why: SINTEF's CoolHeatDC removes the intermediate water loop by condensing the immersion fluid in the heat pump's evaporator, raising the temperature available for district heating. The condenser-evaporator is a compact two-phase heat exchanger, a good fit for printed designs, though SINTEF does not say so. Lab scale only so far. Imperial College London started an EU-funded fellowship (MicroTherM, €276k, 2025-27) to measure the thin liquid layer under bubbles in confined boiling, the physics that sets how well two-phase immersion surfaces perform, and a second one (Micro-PINN, €276k, from November 2026) will reconstruct that layer with physics-informed neural networks. Aalborg University and Heatflow (the start-up behind the printed thermosiphon on the passive two-phase card) start an EU fellowship in October 2026 on injecting a second liquid to make bubbles on purpose in two-phase immersion baths.

applicability.reason: SINTEF targets data centres; the printed heat-exchanger angle is our inference.

trl.reason: Lab tests and techno-economic modelling.

cards.barriers: Two-phase dielectric fluids face PFAS restrictions in Europe.

cards.headline: Heatwaves and UK AI compute: is heat rejection sized for new summers?
cards.problem: UK heatwaves (37.3 C June 2026 record) push dry coolers and chillers past their design ambient.
cards.technology: Heat rejection sized for higher ambient, and liquid cooling that runs warmer.
cards.why: Cambridge's Dawn AI supercomputer went offline during the June 2026 heatwave. The cause was not confirmed as thermal, but it raises a UK-specific question about design ambient temperatures. A problem signal rather than a technology; worth watching for a confirmed cause.

applicability.reason: The article does not confirm a thermal cause; the heat-rejection link is our reading.

trl.reason: Problem signal.

cards.barriers: Cause unconfirmed.
